KEY MESSAGE 1...Hot and humid conditions are expected to 
persist through Tuesday of next week, though an improvement in 
humidity is expected Sunday into Monday. A Heat Advisory is in 
effect for portions of the area through today.

A relatively stagnant synoptic pattern will remain in place 
across our region. Quasi zonal mid and upper level flow will be
in place through the middle of next week as Bermuda high 
pressure persists offshore. This will keep a steady stream of 
very warm and moist air in place across the region through the 
period.

A prolonged period of hot and humid conditions will continue 
for the next several days. With dewpoints remaining in the low
to mid 70s and highs in the upper 80s to low 90s today, heat 
indices will again be near 100 degrees this afternoon, mainly 
along and southeast of the I-95 corridor. A weak cold frontal 
passage Sunday will help usher in slightly drier air and allow 
dewpoints to mix out during the afternoon hours both Sunday and 
Monday. This will give some slight reprieve from the excessive 
humidity, though highs will still be in the upper 80s to low or 
even mid 90s. The lower dewpoints Sunday and Monday will result
in maximum heat indices mainly in the mid to upper 90s, though
could get near 100 degrees in Delmarva and far southern New
Jersey. Since the forecast is decidedly below Heat Advisory
criteria, we've opted not to extend it to cover additional days
at this time, though it will still be hot and humid.

A Heat Advisory remains in effect through 8 PM this evening for
portions of southeastern Pennsylvania, portions of New Jersey, 
and northern Delware.

Moisture advection will return again by Tuesday ahead of 
another cold front, and slightly more humid conditions should 
return for Tuesday. A somewhat stronger cold front looks to come
through late Tuesday or Wednesday, which will help bring a 
slight reduction in temperatures. Highs by Wednesday and 
Thursday are mostly in the mid to upper 80s, which will be 
closer to average for early to mid August.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms
are forecast to develop this afternoon and evening. Sunday 
still looks to be largely dry, then daily chances for showers 
and thunderstorms will return Monday and into the middle of next
week. There is at least a marginal risk for localized heavy 
rainfall leading to flash flooding and locally damaging wind 
gusts with any stronger thunderstorms that develop.

The evolution of today's convection remains a little unclear
still. A feature of interest will be the convective complex
currently across the upper Ohio Valley early this morning. While
that activity should weaken later this morning, it's remnants
will likely become a focus for forcing diurnally driven
convection in our region later today as it drifts eastward. 
CAMs still suggesting isolated to scattered thunderstorms 
developing across the area this afternoon and evening. Synoptic 
forcing isn't as strong as what we had Friday, though the 
remnant dynamics from the convection upstream could give us 
better forcing at the mesoscale level. So we could see more 
widespread thunderstorms than CAMs suggest, but not super 
confident on that at the moment. PWATs look slightly lower than 
today, but overall the thermodynamics appear similar to Friday
(2000-3000 J/kg CAPE). Notably, mean flow is more westerly and 
a bit stronger than Friday, so deep layer wind shear is a little
stronger in the 25-30 kt range. This will pose more of a large 
hail risk compared to Friday as well, but damaging winds will be
the main threat with any stronger storms. Locally heavy 
rainfall leading to flash flooding is also possible, but 
thinking the stronger flow aloft should keep storms moving 
faster and pose slightly less of a flash flood risk.

We remain in a Marginal (level 1 out of 4) Risk for excessive 
rainfall from WPC. SPC has maintained the Marginal (level 1 out
of 5) Risk for severe thunderstorms for most of our area.

We look to have a weak cold frontal passage by Sunday, ushering
in slightly drier air. This combined with subtle subsidence 
aloft will help briefly limit convection potential on Sunday,
though cannot completely rule out some isolated sea breeze
convection in the afternoon.

Better support for forcing aloft will return by late Monday as 
mean flow shifts more westerly and mid level flow increases.
At this point though, it appears the greater threat of storms 
will be to our northwest on Monday where SPC has a Marginal Risk
highlighted. Still could get some isolated storms, but Monday is
trending drier locally as the lingering lower dewpoints should
limit our instability a bit. Better moisture and instability
return by Tuesday though, along with better storm chances. With
the stronger mid level flow aloft, severe thunderstorms still 
look to be a greater threat compared to flash flooding, but
these details remain unclear.
